entries.1:1: This verse introduces the whole book as a message from God about the city of Nineveh, received in a vision by a man named Nahum. It reminds the reader that what follows is presented as God's word, not just one man's opinion.
entries.1:2: God cares deeply about his own honor and does not ignore wrongdoing; he is angry at evil and will act against those who set themselves against him. The reader should take sin seriously, because God does not shrug it off.
entries.1:3: God is patient and slow to lose his temper, but his patience does not mean he will let guilt go unpunished, and his power is shown in storms and clouds. The reader can trust that God is both merciful and just, and that no wrong is simply forgotten.
entries.1:4: God's command is so powerful that he can dry up seas and rivers, and even lush regions like Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon wither before him. The reader should see that nothing in nature is stronger than God's word.
entries.1:5: The mountains shake and the earth breaks apart when God appears, showing that even the most solid things cannot stand before him. The reader is reminded that God is far greater than anything created.
entries.1:6: No one can stand up to God when his anger is stirred, and his fury is pictured as fire that shatters rock. The reader should understand that opposing God is a serious and hopeless position.
entries.1:7: Even while describing judgment, this verse says God is good and a safe shelter in hard times, and he knows and protects those who trust him. The reader can run to God for safety rather than try to hide from him.
entries.1:8: God will sweep away his enemies like a flood and drive those who hate him into darkness. The reader should see that God's judgment is thorough and that no enemy of his will escape.
entries.1:9: Any plan made against God will be stopped before it succeeds, and his enemies will not get a second chance to rise up. The reader should not fear plots against God's purposes, because they will fail.
entries.1:10: The enemies are pictured as tangled thorns or drunks, but they will burn up quickly like dry grass. The reader should see that even people who seem strong and dangerous are fragile before God.
entries.1:11: Someone from Nineveh has been plotting evil against God, but those plans are worthless. The reader is reminded that evil schemes against God amount to nothing in the end.
entries.1:12: God says that the time of trouble he allowed for his people is over, and their enemies will not trouble them again. The reader can take hope that hard seasons under God's discipline do not last forever.
entries.1:13: God promises to break the heavy yoke and chains that have been weighing his people down. The reader can look to God as the one who sets people free from what holds them captive.
entries.1:14: God has ordered that Nineveh's name will end and its idols will be destroyed, leaving it disgraced. The reader should see that God opposes both cruel power and false gods, and he will bring them down.
entries.1:15: A messenger comes over the mountains bringing good news of peace, and God's people are told to keep their festivals and promises because their enemy is gone for good. The reader is encouraged to celebrate and stay faithful, since God has removed the threat.
entries.2:1: An attacker is coming against the city, so the people are told to watch closely and gather their strength. It means danger is near and being alert and prepared is urgent, even if it may not be enough.
entries.2:2: God promises to restore the people of Jacob and Israel, because their enemies had destroyed them like a ruined vineyard. It means God sees the damage done to his people and intends to bring them back.
entries.2:3: The attacking soldiers and chariots are described in vivid red and fire, ready for battle. It means the enemy army is fierce and prepared, and the scene is one of frightening power.
entries.2:4: The chariots race through the streets and squares like flashing fire and thunder. It means the attack is fast and chaotic, and the city cannot easily stop it.
entries.2:5: The enemy commander calls his officers, but they stumble on the way as they rush to the wall and set up its cover. It means even the attackers are struggling, yet they still press on toward the city.
entries.2:6: The city's river gates are broken open and the palace is swept away by water. It means the city's defenses fail and its royal center collapses.
entries.2:7: The queen is stripped and carried off, while her servant girls mourn like cooing doves and beat their breasts. It means the city's leaders are humiliated and the women grieve in deep distress.
entries.2:8: Nineveh is compared to a leaking pool whose water drains away, and though people shout for them to stay, no one turns back. It means the city's people are fleeing and cannot be held together.
entries.2:9: The attackers are told to take silver and gold, since the city's treasures are endless. It means Nineveh's wealth is now free for the taking by its enemies.
entries.2:10: The city is emptied and stripped bare, and its people are weak with fear, shaking knees, and pale faces. It means total ruin has come and everyone is terrified.
entries.2:11: The prophet asks where the lions' den is now, the place where lions once lived safely with their cubs. It means the proud and powerful city that once seemed untouchable has been brought down.
entries.2:12: The lion once filled its den with prey for its cubs and lionesses. It means Nineveh had grown rich by violence and plunder, storing up what it took from others.
entries.2:13: God declares he is against the city, will burn its chariots, and will end its violent power and proud roar. It means God himself opposes those who live by cruelty, and their strength will not last.
entries.3:1: God pronounces doom on Nineveh, a city guilty of lies, violence, and endless killing. It warns the reader that cruelty and bloodshed do not go unnoticed by God.
entries.3:2: The scene shifts to the sounds of an attacking army—whips cracking, chariot wheels rumbling, horses charging. It shows that judgment is arriving swiftly and loudly.
entries.3:3: The attack brings swords, spears, and piles of dead bodies so many that attackers stumble over them. It pictures the terrible cost of the city's violence coming back on itself.
entries.3:4: Nineveh is compared to a seductive prostitute who trapped nations and families with lies and secret schemes. It warns that manipulation and deceit, however successful, will be exposed.
entries.3:5: God himself declares he is against the city and will strip it bare for all nations to see. It means no power can hide its shame when God acts against it.
entries.3:6: God will make the city utterly disgraced and put on display for everyone to see. It shows that pride and cruelty end in public humiliation, not glory.
entries.3:7: Everyone who sees the ruined city will flee from it, and no one will mourn or comfort it. It means a city that caused so much pain will find no sympathy when it falls.
entries.3:8: The city is asked whether it is any better than Thebes, a strong city surrounded by water. It reminds the reader that no amount of natural defense makes anyone safe from judgment.
entries.3:9: Thebes had Ethiopia and countless Egyptians as allies, plus other nations helping her. It shows that even great alliances cannot protect a city God has decided to bring down.
entries.3:10: Yet Thebes was captured anyway—her children killed, her leaders divided by lot or chained. It means the strongest city's fate is a warning of what awaits Nineveh.
entries.3:11: Nineveh will be left staggering and helpless, looking for somewhere to hide from its enemies. It means false confidence will collapse into fear when trouble comes.
entries.3:12: The city's fortresses will be like ripe figs that fall into an open mouth at the slightest shake. It means its defenses will give way easily, with no real resistance.
entries.3:13: The city's fighting men will be as weak as women, and its gates will stand open with their bars burned. It means the city's protection will fail completely.
entries.3:14: The people are told to store water and strengthen their defenses for a siege, working hard at the brickworks. It shows desperate effort to prepare, even though it will not be enough.
entries.3:15: Fire and sword will still destroy them, no matter how many they multiply like locusts. It means sheer numbers cannot save a people from the judgment coming on them.
entries.3:16: Their traders had multiplied like the stars of heaven, making the city rich and busy. It reminds the reader that wealth and commerce are no shield when destruction comes.
entries.3:17: The city's guards and officials are like locusts that vanish when the sun rises. It means those who seemed to protect the city will disappear when danger arrives.
entries.3:18: The king of Assyria's leaders are asleep and his people are scattered with no one to gather them. It means the empire's shepherds have failed and its people are left helpless.
entries.3:19: The city's wound is fatal and cannot be healed, and everyone who hears of its fall will celebrate. It means a long record of evil finally brings an end that others welcome.
